items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 2, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including acting President Iliana Yotova’s victory in Bulgaria’s presidential runoff, a multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky ending with no violations, US President Donald Trump prioritizing diplomatic engagement with Iran despite pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to launch military strikes immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, and the arrest of more than 200 people in Germany following Gen Z protests. Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Yotova was heading for a decisive victory in a presidential runoff against her pro-Western challenger, according to exit polls. Completed parallel counts by five major polling agencies put Yotova’s share of the vote at between 56.6% and 58.2% compared with 38.6% to 40.6% for Andrey Gyurov. “We accept the results, no matter how surprising they are,” Gyurov told a press conference in Sofia, adding that while the campaign is ending, the responsibility is not. Yotova, a longtime figure within the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), improved on her first-round result from last weekend, when she finished with 34.76% against Gyurov at 31.95%. Her campaign emphasized no additional arms support for Ukraine and instead called for peace through a diplomatic solution, in contrast to her rival. - Oleshky ceasefire between Russia, Ukraine ends with no violations reported A multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky ended late Sunday with no violations reported by either side. The truce, announced by US first lady Melania Trump to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, took effect Tuesday and was extended beyond Oleshky, in the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys. Trump said the ceasefire had given residents the freedom to move and access to food, clean water, and medicine, as well as "a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack." “Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace,” she wrote on US social media platform X. ... - More than 200 arrests in Germany after Gen Z protests German police arrested more than 200 people after violent clashes erupted in several cities following largely peaceful Generation Z demonstrations demanding better education funding and social policies. The unrest broke out in Hamburg, Frankfurt and Berlin after radical groups staged smaller demonstrations, erecting barricades and clashing with police. The main daytime demonstrations, organized by the Gen Z Regelt initiative across more than 30 cities, brought tens of thousands of young people into the streets to demand greater investment in education, action to ease the rising cost of living and an end to plans to reinstate compulsory military service. After dark, radical groups staged smaller demonstrations in other parts of the cities, erecting barricades as the situation escalated once police moved to contain them. Some activists threw stones, bottles and firecrackers at officers, who responded with water cannons and special units in several locations.

items.title: Headlines for November 02, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Democratic Congressmember Stevens Endorses MAGA Republican Rogers in Michigan’s Senate Election Nov 02, 2026 In Michigan, Democratic Congressmember Haley Stevens switched her endorsement from progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Trump-backed MAGA Republican Mike Rogers just two days before an election that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Stevens narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary back in August. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the move “a despicable betrayal,” and several members of Stevens’s staff resigned, including her chief of staff. On Sunday, Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit. The DNC’s Black Caucus chair Virgie Rollins said in a statement, “We are dismayed that Congresswoman Haley Stevens has revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.” ... ## Federal Judge Orders Trump Admin to Halt Pressure Campaign Against Election Officials Nov 02, 2026 A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to halt its recent pressure campaign against election officials nationwide. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson said in her ruling Friday, “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters.” According to the ruling, the Justice and Homeland Security departments cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters or halt ballot processing. Judge Thompson also blocked threats of criminal prosecutions against election officials. In Alaska, a federal judge has rejected a Trump administration lawsuit that was seeking to block certification of Tuesday’s Senate election if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. The Justice Department claimed a second candidate on the ballot with a nearly identical name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., was running to confuse voters, and asked the court to set aside and investigate ballots cast for him.

items.title: US manufacturing picks up in October; input prices stay high By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid strong domestic demand, keeping inflation at the factory gate elevated. Despite the unexpected improvement reported by the Institute for Supply Management on Monday, sentiment among manufacturers remained overwhelmingly downbeat, with some complaining that "economic policies coming out of Washington continue to weigh on business conditions," and others saying the situation was "making it impossible to make sound long-term decisions." They were likely referring to rising prices for a range of commodities including energy, stemming from the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran. A recent escalation in the trade war with Canada was also cited by manufacturers as a constraint. The inflation fallout from the Middle East conflict has also helped depress consumer sentiment, culminating in broad disapproval of President Donald Trump’s stewardship of the economy. Discontent over the rising cost of living is likely to determine control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Economists cautioned that rising interest rates and declining inflation-adjusted household income would hamper manufacturing activity next year, especially the segments not exposed to the artificial intelligence spending frenzy. ... The ISM said its manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index increased to 55.5 last month from 54.5 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI would stay at 54.5. The PMI has stayed above the 50 threshold this year, indicating growth in manufacturing, a sector that accounts for about 9.4% of the economy. A measure of production at factories jumped 2.3 percentage points to 59 last month, the highest reading since November 2021. ... Activity is being driven by robust consumer spending and business spending on AI. The government reported last week that domestic demand grew at its fastest pace in more than five years in the third quarter. The overall economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter after expanding at a 2.2% pace in the April-June period, even as the war in the Middle East stoked inflation. The ISM survey’s new orders measure edged up to 55.5 from 55.3 in September, with exports also rising. Factory inventories also increased. The government’s advance GDP report showed that business inventories rebounded last quarter after having been drawn down for five ... The survey’s supplier deliveries index inched up to 59.1 from 59.0 in September. A reading above 50 indicates slower deliveries. Suppliers’ delivery performance to manufacturing organizations slowed for the 11th straight month. Among the products that remained in short supply were aluminum, copper, electrical and electronic components, and memory chips. Strained supply chains meant factories continued to pay more for inputs. The survey’s gauge of prices paid for inputs eased to a still-high 75.2 from 77.9 in September, supporting economists’ views that inflation will continue to run above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target into 2027. Prices continued to rise for a number of products, including aluminum, copper, diesel fuel, and electronic and memory components. The government last week reported that the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index rose 3.6% year over year in September. It is one of the inflation measures monitored by the US central bank for monetary policy. The Fed last Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate within the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the US central bank to raise borrowing costs in December. ... "Persistent supply constraints and elevated input costs suggest the inflationary blaze remains far from contained," said Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets. "The combination of firmer factory activity and still-hot prices is not a good mix for the Fed."

items.title: The Fed can't fix this inflation. It's a mechanical weight, not a demand problem
items.excerpt: Producer prices are rising 2.6 points faster than consumer prices, the widest gap since 2022, because most of the Iran war's costs haven't reached shoppers yet. The part that has is fuel, and rate hikes can't make fuel cheaper. The Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks what US businesses get for the goods and services they sell, rose 6.3% through September. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7%. In February, the last full month before the Iran war, the gap between them was about a point. It's now 2.6 points, the widest since April 2022. Most of the war's costs still fall on businesses, and shoppers pay at the pump. The Federal Reserve (Fed) raised its rate to 3.75-4.00% in September and held it in October, with two members voting for another hike. The number that matters most for inflation is the price of Brent, the main global Oil price, and no one at the Fed sets it. ## Seven months of war, a tenth of a point outside energy Energy prices, which cover gasoline and the power and fuel used in homes, rose 20.4% through September, and gasoline alone rose 34.2%. Energy makes up about 7% of the CPI, so it added about 1.3 percentage points to the 3.7% total. In February it added almost nothing. Everything else barely changed. Prices outside food and energy, often called underlying inflation, were up 2.6%, a tenth of a point faster than in February. Food prices are rising more slowly than they were before the war. So almost all of the 1.3-point rise in inflation since February is the fuel bill, and with Brent trading near its highest since mid-2022, that bill hasn't gone away.

items.title: U.S. Economy Grows 3.4% as 3.7% Inflation Keeps Costs in Focus | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: The U.S. economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, while inflation reached 3.7% over the year through September as voters prepared to weigh economic conditions in Tuesday’s midterm elections. ... The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) estimated real gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a 3.4% annual rate from July through September, compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. Investment, consumer spending and government spending contributed to the gain; lower exports partly offset it as imports increased. BEA data show real personal consumption expenditures grew at a 3.8% annual rate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September from August and 3.7% over the 12 months through September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year. The CPI gasoline index climbed 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of that month’s increase in the overall index. Annual inflation had fallen from 9.1% in June 2022 to 2.3% in April 2025 before rising again; the lower rate meant prices were rising more slowly, not falling overall. The Conference Board’s Consumer Confidence Index rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, from 84.2 in September. The board said confidence remained on a long-term downward trend and consumers planned to reduce spending on services and durable goods over the next six months. Its six-month moving average rose only among consumers younger than 35 and households with incomes of $100,000 or more. Fergus McCormick, a senior economist for Global Indicators at The Conference Board, said consumers “continued to express frustration with rising costs.” AAA’s national averages on Nov. 1 were $4.1732 per gallon for regular gasoline and $6.3039 for diesel, compared with $3.0380 and $3.6862 a year earlier.

items.title: 2026 election live updates as Supreme Court denies Trump bid to separate California ballots, candidates make final pitches
items.excerpt: Updated on: November 2, 2026 / 6:27 PM EST / CBS News ## What to know leading up to Election Day 2026: - Over 57 million Americans have already voted early ahead of Election Day, this Tuesday, Nov. 3. - As the campaign season comes to a close, President Trump delivered his final scheduled remarks of the 2026 midterm elections, saying Republicans "gave this a very strong shot." - The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's last-ditch bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots. - A rift between Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and primary rival Haley Stevens spilled into public view Sunday, as Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers. Democrats condemned Stevens, though Rep. Debbie Dingell argued it's "galvanizing" voters toward El-Sayed. ... ## Judge rejects request from Democrats to block DOJ from ordering election workers to remove alleged noncitizens A federal judge on Monday denied a request from several Democratic groups to bar the Justice Department from asking state and local election officials to remove alleged noncitizens from their voter rolls or segregate their ballots. In his ruling, U.S. District Judge James Boasberg wrote that the Justice Department is "attempting to browbeat" states into removing people from voter rolls, and noted that states have raised concerns about the accuracy of the lists of alleged noncitizens assembled by the federal government. But he ultimately found that the plaintiffs did not have standing to sue. "Even extraordinary merits questions cannot justify the extraordinary relief of a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order if those seeking it lack standing," Boasberg wrote. He also noted that the government's "attempted interference has yet to alter a single rule or process governing the upcoming election," in part because state officials have resisted the Trump administration's efforts. Earlier Monday, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request to force California to separate around 20,000 mail ballots from people it claims are noncitizens, after lower courts also refused to intervene. And in a separate lawsuit brought by labor groups, a California judge last week ordered the government to stop trying to "intimidate" and "threaten" election workers by ordering them to separate out ballots and dangling criminal charges if they don't comply.

Stevens narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary back in August. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the move “a despicable betrayal,” and several members of Stevens’s staff resigned, including her chief of staff. On Sunday, Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit. The DNC’s Black Caucus chair Virgie Rollins said in a statement, “We are dismayed that Congresswoman Haley Stevens has revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.” And Drop Site News reports that a spokesperson for the Mike Rogers campaign, Abigail Ronson, is a registered foreign agent for Israel, as well as another campaign staffer, Jesse Stokes. In the hours following Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers, El-Sayed raised $1.2 million. This is Dr. El-Sayed speaking on Sunday. ... ## Federal Judge Orders Trump Admin to Halt Pressure Campaign Against Election Officials Nov 02, 2026 A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to halt its recent pressure campaign against election officials nationwide. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson said in her ruling Friday, “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters.” According to the ruling, the Justice and Homeland Security departments cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters or halt ballot processing. Judge Thompson also blocked threats of criminal prosecutions against election officials. In Alaska, a federal judge has rejected a Trump administration lawsuit that was seeking to block certification of Tuesday’s Senate election if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. The Justice Department claimed a second candidate on the ballot with a nearly identical name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., was running to confuse voters, and asked the court to set aside and investigate ballots cast for him. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in her ruling that the federal government “offers no rebuttal to the concerns regarding preservation of the secrecy of voting and provides no explanation of how its request for ballot segregation and a court-ordered investigation by law enforcement officers into certain voters’ intent could be implemented while preserving the secrecy of the ballot.” This follows The New York Times’s recent report that operatives from the Peltola campaign had recruited Daniel J. Sullivan to run to peel votes away from the incumbent Republican senator. Peltola has denied the claims.

items.excerpt: Updated: Monday, November 2, 2026, 15:32 [IST] ... ## ENTERTAINMENT NEWS LIVE UPDATES - NOVEMBER 2, 2026 One of the biggest talking points is Bollywood superstar Shah Rukh Khan celebrating his 61st birthday today. Yes, you read that right! On the special occasion, the actor has gifted fans the first song Tu Mil Jaaye from his hugely anticipated film King. Also, Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana Part 1 is just a few days away from hitting theatres and has been creating immense buzz among the moviegoers. The film's advance booking have opened fully now and it is already breaking a lot of records and is outpacing Ranbir Kapoor and Yash's biggest hits - Animal and KGF Chapter 2, respectively. ... ## King First Song Tu Mil Jaaye Released On SRK's Birthday Shah Rukh Khan has reunited with Deepika Padukone, and fans have another reason to celebrate. The superstar released the first song from his much-hyped film King at midnight on November 2, coinciding with his birthday celebrations. Titled Tu Mil Jaaye, the track brings back the popular on-screen pairing and their fans are elated. Nov 02, 2026, 9:50 am IST ... Shah Rukh Khan turned 61 on Monday (November 2), but his birthday celebrations looked a little different this year. The Bollywood superstar did not make his usual midnight appearance outside Mannat, his iconic Mumbai residence in Bandra, where hundreds of fans gather every year to catch a glimpse of him. With Mannat currently undergoing major reconstruction and expansion work, SRK could not follow his usual birthday ritual. However, the actor made sure his fans still received a special birthday surprise. A handwritten note from Shah Rukh was displayed on a giant screen outside his bungalow for fans who had gathered there. Posters of his upcoming film King were also spotted outside Mannat, adding to the excitement among fans waiting to celebrate their favourite superstar's birthday.
